The biggest missing pieces are **what counts as acceptable performance, whether simulation predicts your real machines, and who will accept that evidence**. The booklet found no universal physical-test percentage or simulation-error tolerance you can simply adopt; those must be justified for your intended use and agreed with reviewers. [f187, f275]

“Not found” means **not found in the published research**, not necessarily nonexistent or unavailable from a supplier.

## 1. Acceptance criteria for the braking function
**Not found:** Statistical acceptance targets in the reviewed off-road standards, published off-road limits for false alarms or unnecessary braking per operating hour, or the nuisance-alarm rate operators will accept. [f324, f248, f249]

**You need to establish:** Your own acceptable miss rate, nuisance-intervention limits and statistical demonstration criteria—separately for advisory warnings, urgent warnings, speed reduction and full braking. Matching the existing warning system is not enough: automatic braking is a different safety function. [f2124, f10417]

## 2. Real braking behaviour and intervention timing
**Not found:** Modern brake-delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers and haul trucks; validated simulated stopping distances on gravel, mud, ice or slopes; or an off-road case quantitatively comparing simulation-tuned brake thresholds with field results. [f252, f253, f251]

**You need to establish:** Measured latency, brake build-up and stopping performance across relevant payloads, grades and surfaces, followed by physical confirmation of the thresholds selected in simulation. The booklet recommends a calibrated stopping model using those measured quantities—not assumed generic braking behaviour. [f146, f251, f253]

## 3. Sensor-model accuracy in difficult conditions
**Not found:** A validated radar or camera dust model with a reported error metric, or off-road sensor-model fidelity thresholds. The research also found no validated vibration-to-sensor-output model, and no adverse-weather or off-road validation of thermal or ultrasonic simulation. [f254, f5220, f4431, f4435]

**You need to establish:** How closely each relevant simulated sensor matches your actual hardware and mounting, which errors are acceptable, and the conditions outside which its results cannot support a safety claim. Real sensor hardware is needed to judge virtual-output credibility. [f736, f5220]

## 4. Human response to warnings
**Not found:** Representative operator reaction times to proximity warnings or a validated off-road operator model. [f247, f250]

**You need to establish:** Evidence—or explicitly conservative bounds—for the operator-response assumptions used in warning-to-braking timing. Existing warning-system field history can support inputs and submodels, but cannot validate the new closed-loop braking chain. [f247, f250, f191]

## 5. What constitutes sufficient coverage
**Not found:** A method or standard prescribing the number of virtual environments needed, or public exposure distributions showing how often relevant off-road operating conditions occur. [f255, f7422]

**You need to establish:** A defensible coverage argument: which operating conditions and encounters matter, how they are represented, and how your own field exposure supports their weighting. There is no published environment count that, by itself, demonstrates completeness. [f255, f7422]

## 6. Reuse across machines and sensor positions
**Not found:** A published approach for transferring perception evidence across sensor mounting positions, or a published off-road example of validated variant transfer. [f370, f7574]

**You need to establish:** Where machines and installations are sufficiently similar, where they differ, and what targeted physical tests bridge those differences. The booklet treats reuse as **extending a validation domain with evidence**, not inheriting validation automatically; its recommended approach is a parameterized family model tested at envelope corners, plus bridge tests for new variants. [f189, f190]

## 7. Acceptance of virtual evidence
**Not found:** A published commitment by an off-road regulator or notified body to accept virtual evidence, or notified-body lead times for a machine-learning safety component under the Machinery Regulation. [f258, f259]

**You need to establish:** Direct agreement on the proposed evidence package, model-validity limits, retained physical tests and assessment schedule. The amount of physical testing that remains depends on what reviewers require to trust the virtual results—not a generic substitution ratio. [f275, f187]

## 8. A credible cost and schedule
**Not found:** Published effort, staffing, cost or timeline figures for building the required off-highway virtual-validation capability; a public total-cost build-versus-buy study; or even a statement by an off-road manufacturer that simulation, replay or hardware-in-the-loop shortened validation time. The research found no case in any industry of a new automatic-braking function going from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about **four months**. [f256, f199, f257, f58]

**You need to establish:** Your own implementation estimates and measured productivity, rather than claiming generic virtualization savings. You also need to investigate why the previous programme took three to four years: the research had no published account of your actual bottlenecks. [f256, f11185]

### A separate gap: your internal starting point
The research used **no internal recordings, sensor specifications, site videos or documents**. Your machine types, sensors, software maturity and recording inventory were therefore unknown—not findings that these assets are absent. Establishing that inventory may close some gaps immediately; the others require supplier evidence, assessor agreement or your own experiments. [f7, f8]

results.answer:
A simulation credibility report should establish **which decisions the results can support, within what limits, and with what remaining uncertainty**—not merely present successful simulation runs. The booklet’s core reporting set is a best estimate, uncertainty statement, factor-by-factor credibility assessment, declared validity envelope, separated calibration/validation/confirmation data, and retained failed validation cases. [f7525, f193]

## Recommended report contents

1. **Decision, intended use and claims**  
   State the exact question being answered, the role simulation plays in the decision, and the consequence of a wrong result. Trace each safety claim to its evidence; identify whether that evidence is virtual, physical or mixed. Credibility effort should scale with decision risk. [f7525, f10907]

2. **Model and configuration identification**  
   Identify the sensor and firmware versions, machine and mounting configuration, calibration conditions, environmental parameters, reference instrumentation and its measurement uncertainty. Record any parameter tuning performed using validation data. These are the booklet’s recommended minimum particulars for the off-road sensor-model credibility file. [f4840]

3. **Verification evidence**  
   Show that the code and numerical solution have been verified—not just that outputs resemble measurements. Keep verification distinct from validation against physical data. [f7525]

4. **Validation design and physical evidence**  
   Identify separately the data used for **calibration**, independent **validation**, and genuinely **withheld confirmation**. Include physical end-to-end confirmation: validating individual submodels does not remove the need to validate at the same system boundary as the safety claim. The booklet recommends retaining assessor-chosen confirmation runs, including at least one per EMESRT scenario family; that is a project recommendation, not a universal rule. [f7589, f8195, f8197, f7887]

5. **Results, acceptance criteria and uncertainty**  
   Present best estimates, the metric and acceptance threshold, observed errors and confidence intervals, and the risk of acting on the results. State the required credibility-factor thresholds in advance, based on decision criticality—not after seeing the results. [f193, f4840, f8001, f14588]

6. **Factor-by-factor credibility assessment**  
   For each factor, report the required and achieved level, supporting evidence, rationale, assessor independence and limitations. If using NASA’s approach, factors are rated separately on a **0–4 scale**; do not add them into one overall score that could conceal a weakness. [f8001, f14580, f14588]

7. **Validity envelope and restrictions**  
   Show a map distinguishing **physically validated**, **conditionally supported/interpolated**, and **unsupported/extrapolated** regions, with the physical evidence beneath each. Identify known invalid regions rather than offering a blanket statement such as “the model is 95% accurate.” [f8019, f8012, f4840]

8. **Failures, discrepancies and dissent**  
   Retain failed validation cases. Document biases, unexplained residuals, non-conservative predictions, workarounds and restrictions. Disclose dissenting technical opinions alongside the results rather than hiding them in internal review records. [f7590, f8014, f9741]

9. **Review decision and reproducible appendices**  
   State the remaining uncertainty, who has authority to accept it, and exactly which physical tests may be replaced by simulation. Provide enough supporting material for a specialist to reproduce or challenge the work. Assessors should approve **specific test substitutions**, not “virtual testing” as a category. [f10907, f11159, f9997]

## Put a one-page credibility map at the front

For every safety claim, show: **claim → virtual/physical/mixed evidence → real-world data validating the model → remaining uncertainty → acceptance authority**. This is the booklet’s recommended common view for all reviewers. [f10907]

## What this does—and does not—guarantee

There is **no universal acceptable simulation error or mandatory physical-test percentage** in the credibility frameworks checked; acceptance must be justified for the particular decision. [f7534, f7535]

For heavy off-road collision mitigation, the booklet found **no standard explicitly accepting simulation instead of physical collision-avoidance or automatic-braking tests**. Full paid standards texts could not all be checked, so “not found” does not mean “prohibited”—but a well-written report alone does not establish permission to substitute tests. [f7539, f7544, f11159]

results.answer:
Establish a **separate, independent record of what was present, where and when**, then replay the existing warning system against it. The booklet recommends a hybrid of **surveyed targets, reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS, and human-audited automatic labels**—not the warning system’s own detections used as truth. [f94, f99, f100]

### 1. Check what the recordings can support

Before labeling, audit whether the logs contain synchronized raw sensor streams; machine speed, gear, steering and articulation; brake/retarder state; relevant payload; calibration; and weather/site metadata. These are the recommended inputs for a defensible replay record. [f520]

If you recorded only object lists or processed detections, you cannot rerun a different perception algorithm because the raw measurements are gone. Replay conclusions also apply only to the sensor set, mounting positions and scenarios actually recorded. [f5652, f5166]

**Do not fill missing truth with the production detector’s output:** objects it missed would disappear from both the predictions and the supposed truth, making the baseline artificially good. [f99]

### 2. Define the truth record before creating labels

For each relevant object and encounter, the reference should establish:

- Object identity and class.
- 3D position and trajectory in a common machine or world coordinate frame.
- Machine pose and velocity.
- Timestamps sufficient to determine distance, hazard-zone entry and warning timing. [f5358]

Write an annotation specification covering object taxonomy, the reference point on each object, visibility and occlusion, whether a partially hidden person counts as a detection opportunity, temporal continuity, uncertainty, and how labeler disagreements are resolved. This is the booklet’s **expert recommendation**, rather than simply “draw boxes on video.” [f5401]

### 3. Build truth using three complementary methods

- **Surveyed or instrumented targets:** anchor physical accuracy and calibrate the other truth-generation methods. [f100]
- **Reference lidar plus RTK-GNSS/INS:** provide continuous distance, position and timing reference during recorded encounters. [f100]
- **Offline automatic labeling with human review:** cover recording volume, with stratified human audits and uncertainty flags—not an unaudited labeling oracle. Use the audited subset to measure label error. [f5383, f5418]

The hybrid recommendation draws substantially on **independent on-road evidence**; it should not be presented as an already qualified reference stack for all off-road conditions. [f100, f5399]

### 4. Qualify the reference itself

Ground truth is a measurement system, not an infallible answer. Its target-position, machine-pose, speed and timing uncertainties must be substantially smaller than the acceptance margins being assessed, supported by calibrated reference chains and an uncertainty budget. [f7473]

Check synchronization explicitly: a timing offset between sensors and truth can look like a perception error. Position error directly shifts measured warning distance. [f11243, f5421]

Include a **“truth unavailable or ambiguous”** state. Dust, occlusion or reference-sensor failure must not be forced into confident labels. The booklet found no published validation of one reference stack spanning the full combination of quarry/mining dust, snow, mud, darkness and large-machine occlusion. [f5394, f5399]

### 5. Score the warning baseline by encounter

Use **independent encounters, not frames**, as the analysis unit. Report:

- Detection probability and missed encounters, stratified by object class.
- First-detection distance/time, track persistence, and range/position error where available.
- Warnings per hazard, missed hazards, false and nuisance alarms per hour, and warning time-to-collision against a defined common hazard zone—for example, the ISO 21815-3 risk area. [f5425, f5429, f5431, f5210]

Give detection probability with a binomial confidence interval for each safety-critical grouping; correlated frames must not inflate the sample count. Report audited **label precision and recall alongside the performance metrics**, so uncertainty in the reference remains visible. [f5454, f5461, f5422]

The practical dividing line is therefore **which recorded encounters have defensible independent truth**. A large archive of detections alone is not a trustworthy baseline; a reference-qualified, human-audited encounter corpus is the basis for one. [f99, f5418, f5425]

results.answer:
**Automatic braking is a new safety-control function, not simply a stronger warning.** The stop itself can injure the operator, destabilize the machine or create another collision—even when it prevents the original one. [f114, f5941, f6519]

### Hazards created by the stop

- **Operator jolts and injury risk.** Abrupt braking can produce a violent jolt. Underground workers report “jarring and jolting” stops, although the US regulator says it knows of no injuries resulting from those reported stops. [f6519, f3026, f3027]
- **Load shift or spill.** Hard braking can shift or spill the payload; sudden changes in deceleration also contribute to load movement. [f5941, f13638]
- **Loss of stability or control.** Hazards include rollover, jackknifing or articulation instability, loss of traction and sliding near edges. Slopes, suspended loads and trailer loading are particularly sensitive situations. [f5941, f6519, f1129, f117]
- **A following machine striking the stopped machine.** An unexpected stop can create a rear-end collision hazard rather than eliminate collision risk overall. [f1129]
- **Stopping in an unsafe place.** Nuisance braking can immobilize a machine in a hazardous location or prompt operator counteraction. These are identified as expert-assessed risks in the booklet. [f1129]
- **Rollaway or a second collision after stopping.** Releasing the automatic brake can allow rollback; reset and restart can create another collision if a person remains hidden. The hazard analysis must therefore cover brake holding, operator acknowledgment, release and restart—not just stopping distance. [f6157, f3630]
- **Loss of protection through disabling.** Repeated nuisance interventions can lead operators to disable the system, creating a further safety hazard. [f10441]

### How firmly are these risks established?

The booklet **did not find off-road evidence of automatic-braking-caused load spills, slope instability or rear-end strikes**. These are credible hazards to assess and test, not established off-road incident rates. The reported operator jolts are more directly documented, with the injury caveat above. [f3031, f3026, f3027]

There are practical warnings: **Komatsu’s vendor guidance** tells wheel-loader customers to switch off stop control on slopes, slippery or soft ground, with suspended loads and during trailer loading. Separately, **on-road evidence** reported a **20% increase** in being struck from behind with forward-collision warning plus automatic braking; that figure is not an off-road estimate. [f10420, f3032]

The booklet’s central recommendation is to analyze **missed braking** and **unsafe or unnecessary braking** separately. The objective is not the hardest possible stop: braking must respect traction, stability, brake capacity and payload limits, with a limit on how abruptly deceleration builds. [f118, f5938, f13638]

results.answer:
Use a **calibrated point-mass braking model** for stopping-distance prediction, supplemented by richer models where stability or terrain matters. Automatic braking should be **staged, jerk-limited and constrained by the machine’s current safe envelope**, not set to one universal deceleration. These are the booklet’s engineering recommendations. [f146, f147, f13955, f6280]

### What the vehicle model needs

The core model should include:
- **Measured latency** before braking takes effect.
- **Brake-force build-up**, represented by a ramp or first-order lag.
- **Conservative available deceleration** across grade, payload and surface/friction conditions. [f146, f6069]

Do not use \(v^2/(2a)\) alone: that describes the physical braking component, but misses the delay and build-up contributions. At **5–15 km/h**, delay can account for **half or more of stopping distance**. Grade and payload can change available deceleration by an amount comparable to the deceleration itself. [f6119, f146, f144, f5900]

Keep the online trigger model small and conservative. Use richer offline models to challenge it for **articulation, high-centre-of-gravity stability, axle/track loading, brake hydraulics, hydrostatic-drive behaviour and soft ground**—rather than building one elaborate model for everything. [f6074, f6075, f147]

Calibrate and check the model against your own physical tests. Measure stopping distance both **from the collision-system command** and **from brake-force onset**, so latency cannot disappear into the calibration. The booklet found no universal off-road prediction-error guarantee for any model fidelity. [f13843, f6147, f13842]

### How hard the automatic brake should be

The booklet recommends the following rule, using positive deceleration magnitudes:

\[
a_{\mathrm{command}}
=\min(a_{\mathrm{need}},a_{\mathrm{traction}},
a_{\mathrm{stability}},a_{\mathrm{machine}},a_{\mathrm{load}})
\]

Apply that command with a **jerk-limited ramp**—a limit on how quickly deceleration rises. [f13955, f6318]

- **Early intervention:** controlled partial service braking as the predicted safe margin approaches its minimum, below traction and stability limits. [f6264]
- **Emergency mitigation:** maximum braking consistent with current stability and control constraints when collision is otherwise unavoidable within the conservative stopping envelope. [f6268]
- **Escalation:** use remaining stopping margin **and its uncertainty**, not obstacle range alone. [f6280]

There is **no defensible universal “X m/s²” setting** in the booklet: it found neither a published universal off-road automatic-braking maximum nor a safe numerical jerk threshold for haul trucks, loaders or dozers. Derive limits per machine family and physically test braking with steering/articulation, cross-slope and relevant payloads. [f6308, f3395, f13770]

For context, MOSH surface requirements specify emergency-stop decelerations of **1.9 m/s²** for machines whose top speed exceeds **20 km/h**, and **1.0 m/s²** for others; controlled-stop values are **1.0 or 0.5 m/s²**. These are specified performance values, not universal safe braking caps. Likewise, the **5.0 m/s²** car-AEB demand in UN R152 is **on-road evidence**, not an off-road design target; ISO 3450 is the more relevant braking-acceptance reference here. [f5560, f5561, f6308, f5891, f2572]

results.answer:
**Yes—but reuse must be justified, not assumed.** The booklet’s conclusion is that moving to another machine model or sensor position is **validation-domain extension by similarity plus bridging evidence**, not automatic inheritance of validation. Its recommended approach is a parameterized machine-family model validated at its operating limits, with documented changes and targeted tests for new variants. [f189, f190]

### What can carry over

Evidence for shared software, ECU, interfaces, sensor qualification and common requirements can be reused where it remains applicable. That lets testing concentrate on the differences and worst cases: **common-core evidence plus explicit variant-specific evidence**, rather than blanket family qualification. [f984, f12359]

The transfer argument must cover machine geometry and articulation; mass, inertia and payload; wheel/track and brake dynamics; grade capability; sensor type, firmware, height and angle; occlusion and vibration; sensor-to-brake latency; and environmental effects on perception. [f7907]

### How to justify the transfer

For each change, the safety case should answer three questions:

1. **What changed?** Record a configuration-controlled difference covering geometry, dynamics, sensor installation, software, calibration and environment. [f7908]
2. **Could it affect safety performance?** Use engineering and sensitivity analysis, including uncertainty, to assess whether the difference affects a validated phenomenon or safety output. [f7909]
3. **What additional evidence closes the gap?**
   - Demonstrably irrelevant difference: no additional bridging evidence is needed.
   - Influential difference: targeted component or system tests.
   - New physics or boundary conditions: new full-system physical reference tests. [f7910]

For a new variant **inside the validated parameter range**, the booklet recommends a reduced physical test set—typically **brake calibration plus sensor field-of-view and detection checks at the new mount**. This is expert-recommended practice supported by similarity principles from other sectors, not an established off-road acceptance rule. [f7917]

Outside that range, add physical reference tests at the new boundary and revalidate the affected submodels. Also, proving the smallest and largest machines is not automatically enough: intermediate geometry, articulation, occlusion and braking behavior can produce non-monotonic effects. [f7911, f7919]

### A sensor move is not “just recalibration”

Even with unchanged hardware and software, relocation changes occlusion, viewing angles, ground returns, vibration, range geometry, contamination patterns and apparent object motion during articulation. Sensor position and orientation therefore need their own explicit validated range. [f7921, f7922]

Old raw-log replay cannot establish performance from the new viewpoint: it measures performance only for the sensors, mounting positions and scenarios actually recorded—a limitation the booklet supports with **vendor, on-road evidence**. [f95]

### Limits to the claim

The booklet found **no published off-road variant-transfer example**, no published approach for transferring perception evidence between mounting positions, and no universal acceptable relocation distance or angle. It also found no off-road regulator formally accepting similarity arguments, no ISO rule that testing a fixed number of representative machines validates a family, and no quantified cross-model time savings. [f7574, f260, f7905, f2943, f6683, f261]

So the defensible position is: **reuse the evidence whose applicability you can demonstrate, and test the safety-relevant differences—not necessarily the whole system again, but never nothing merely because the software is unchanged.** [f12359, f7910]

The research gives a **US labor-cost floor of roughly USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist per year**, but **no defensible total team or tool-chain budget**. Commercial simulation prices are mostly quote-only, and even free software can support a **seven-figure annual programme** once specialist labor is included. [f8317, f199, f197, f8318]

## Simulation tools

The few public price points found were these—not a priced, complete validation stack. [f8305]

| Item | Price reported | Important limitation |
|---|---:|---|
| MATLAB | 980 annually / 3,920 perpetual | Presumed USD; unofficial January 2024 list, indicative only. [f8387] |
| Simulink | 1,480 annually / 5,920 perpetual | Same unofficial list and currency caveat. [f8388] |
| RoadRunner | 4,680 annually / 9,360 perpetual | Same unofficial list and currency caveat. [f8389] |
| RoadRunner Scenario | 3,400 annually / 13,600 perpetual | Same unofficial list and currency caveat. [f8390] |
| Duality Falcon education license | USD 20/month | Vendor price for **non-commercial education**, not an industrial deployment. [f8306] |
| NI PXIe controller | About USD 5,200 | Vendor-listed controller price, not a complete hardware-in-the-loop system budget. [f8307] |

The booklet’s conclusion is that **open source reduces license costs, not necessarily total costs**: someone must still build and maintain the tool coupling, assets, scenario database and validation evidence. That assessment draws on vendor evidence. [f196, f8303]

## Virtual-validation team

The research converts US BLS May 2025 median wages into approximate employer compensation using a June 2026 benefits share of **31.5%**—dividing wages by **0.685**. These are expert planning conversions, not occupation-specific forecasts. [f8317, f8783, f8784, f8791]

| Specialist role | Approximate annual employer compensation |
|---|---:|
| QA engineer or mechanical engineer | USD 152,000 [f8786] |
| Electrical engineer | USD 176,000 [f8787] |
| Software developer | USD 199,000 [f8785] |
| Research scientist | USD 205,000 [f8789] |
| Hardware engineer | USD 236,000 [f8788] |
| IT manager | USD 256,000 [f8790] |

These figures **exclude overhead, facilities, recruiting, bonuses, contractors and licenses**. [f8784]

The required skills span simulation integration, machine/soil/braking dynamics, sensor modeling, 3D assets, scenario automation, data/cloud infrastructure, ECU/HIL, statistics and functional safety. This is an expert assessment of disciplines—not a prescription for one employee per discipline. **Team size was not found and was not estimated.** [f8773, f9350]

## Compute

The booklet judges compute relatively cheap compared with engineering labor, while warning that actual simulation speed determines what the money buys. [f8309]

- Third-party trackers listed an **AWS g6e.xlarge with one NVIDIA L40S at about USD 1.861/hour**, on demand in us-east-1. [f8310]
- Its illustrative calculation puts **ten GPU machines running continuously for 122 days at about USD 54,490**, delivering at most about **29,000 GPU-hours**. This is an expert illustration, not a programme operating-cost estimate. [f13546]

## What can actually be budgeted?

The research found **no public off-highway study establishing team size, implementation timeline and total build-versus-buy cost**. Actual annotation, supplier-model licensing and analyst-triage costs were also not found publicly. [f199, f10739]

Its recommendation is therefore to **obtain vendor quotations rather than extrapolate a complete budget from these isolated prices**, and reconfirm every figure at quotation time. [f8308, f9391]
